name: Burnt Siena
lede: Burnt Siena is named for the Tuscan city of Siena, source of an iron-oxide earth pigment that turns from yellow to warm brownish-red once roasted.

sections.title: An earth, roasted
sections.body:
Philip Ball explains that ochres from Siena gained special respect among Renaissance painters [1]. Raw sienna, dug from the ground, is a yellowish iron oxide; roasted over a fire, it turns into the warmer, redder burnt sienna [1]. John Jarman lists it among the earth browns that are, in his words, "cooked to red hot" [2], and Victoria Finlay's colleague-in-trade Coles notes that a moderate roasting heat turns yellow ochre toward orange, and a stronger heat pushes it toward red [3].

Our data carries the color under two spellings, Burnt Siena and the more common Burnt Sienna, and flags the choice as contested [4]. The ISCC-NBS system filed it in 1955, block 40, among the reds [4]; Ridgway's 1886 *Nomenclature of Colors* already carried the name, and his 1912 revision placed it on plate II [4].

sections.title: A warmer swatch than the pigment
sections.body: Its nearest named neighbor is [[brick-orange|Brick Orange]], only 4.1 units away and read as almost the same color [5]; [[windsor-tan|Windsor Tan]] sits close behind, a little duller [5]. The genuine pigment, ground from roasted earth, varies by source and firing time, so any single hex swatch is one sample among many possible burnt siennas [1][3]. [[burnt-orange|Burnt Orange]] and [[alloy-orange|Alloy Orange]] sit further out still, both more vivid or lighter by comparison [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
This color appears in 106 of our 23,781 paintings, about 0.45 percent, more common than 58 percent of our named colors, as photographed [6]. It peaks twice: a broad rise across the 1400s, 1.5 times the expected rate, and a sharper spike in the 1680s, 4.1 times the expected rate [6]. Inside a painting it plays an accent in 87 percent of its appearances [6].

The earliest match is a 1423 panel by Masolino da Panicale, 463 years before Ridgway's 1886 record; our archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first, and a color match on an aged, varnished photograph is not proof that the painter ground real Sienna earth [6]. In printed English the word peaked in the 1930s and rose fastest in that decade, across all its senses [6].
